periods.analysis: Harborview closed 2024-Q3 with General Fund reserves at 19.1%, comfortably above the >=16% green target and consistent with the fiscal discipline expected of an AA-rated coastal city. This first quarter in the current reporting arc gives Council a clean baseline: Finance reconciled the Munis close package on time, and departments submitted Q3 expenditure forecasts through the ClearPoint budget narrative workflow by the October 8 deadline. The result reflects steady property-tax receipts, cautious vacancy budgeting, and controlled summer service overtime across Police beach patrols, Parks marina staffing, and Public Works event support.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green position by keeping the monthly reserve roll-forward in the Council packet, with Finance validating cash, encumbrances, and one-time revenues before publication. Extend the practice that worked this quarter: ask departments to flag any year-end spending accelerations over $75,000 in ClearPoint by the next forecast lock date. Keep the Council message simple and confident: reserves are strong, and we are protecting flexibility without slowing approved service delivery.

periods.analysis: Harborview ended 2024-Q4 at 18.8%, a quarter-over-quarter decrease of 0.3 percentage points from 19.1%, while remaining green and well above the >=16% target. The small planned draw is consistent with year-end activity, including the December transfer timing for the Fleet Replacement set-aside, holiday public-safety overtime, and final invoices on the Seabright Community Center roof project. Importantly, the close was orderly: Finance posted the Q4 reserve calculation after bank reconciliation batch BR-24-12 was completed, and no late departmental adjustments changed the status. For Council, the story is not deterioration; it is controlled use of capacity inside a structurally balanced budget.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by documenting the one-time Q4 uses in the year-end reserve bridge so Council can see exactly why the 0.3-point movement occurred. Extend the deadline discipline by keeping the January 15 accrual cutoff firm for all departments, with exceptions routed through Finance rather than handled offline. Ask Budget staff to tag recurring versus non-recurring Q4 expenditures in the ClearPoint attachment library before the next quarterly review.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, reserves improved to 19.3%, up 0.5 percentage points from 18.8%, keeping Harborview solidly green against the >=16% target. This rebound shows that the year-end drawdown was temporary, with business-license renewals, transient occupancy tax from winter coastal events, and conservative departmental spending all helping rebuild the cushion. Finance also tightened data quality by matching the reserve calculation to trial balance extract TB-25Q1 and requiring department directors to certify forecast tabs before the ClearPoint scorecard refresh. The arc is encouraging: a modest Q4 dip followed by a timely Q1 recovery gives Council evidence that the budget framework is working as designed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain momentum by continuing the director certification step for all Q1-style quarterly closes, because it improved confidence in both the number and the narrative. Extend the green result by creating a short list of eligible one-time uses that would only be considered if reserves remain above 18.5% after the midyear update. Keep watching coastal revenue volatility, especially hotel activity during the shoulder season, and include the trend line in the next Council finance dashboard.

periods.analysis: Harborview reached 19.8% in 2025-Q2, another 0.5 percentage point increase from 19.3%, and remains green with meaningful room above the >=16% policy floor. The second consecutive quarterly increase reflects strong spring sales tax, permitting activity from the Harbor Landing mixed-use cohort, and continued restraint on discretionary operating purchases before fiscal year-end. Finance completed the Q2 reserve schedule two business days ahead of the reporting calendar, which is exactly the kind of on-time cycle that makes departments look prepared in front of Council. At this level, the reserve is not just compliant; it is giving Harborview options for capital timing, grant matches, and emergency readiness without leaning on short-term fixes.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by preserving the current expenditure review for non-essential purchases over $25,000 through fiscal year close. Extend the benefit by pre-identifying Council-approved uses for any audited year-end surplus, prioritizing one-time capital matches and technology stabilization rather than recurring positions. Finance should publish a one-page reserve bridge with the budget adoption materials so the 19.8% result is visible, understandable, and tied to policy.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q3, reserves eased to 19.6%, down 0.2 percentage points from 19.8%, but the measure remains green and comfortably above the >=16% target. The slight movement is consistent with summer operating patterns: lifeguard support reimbursements lagged payroll, Parks carried seasonal irrigation costs, and the City advanced the first installment on the Civic Center HVAC controls contract. The important point for Council is that the decrease is small, explained, and occurring from a strong position after two quarters of growth. Budget staff kept the ClearPoint record clean by attaching the expenditure variance memo for Police, Parks, and Public Works before the quarterly lock, which helps prevent the usual scramble for follow-up questions.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by keeping seasonal cost centers on a separate variance tab through Q4, especially beach operations, harbor patrol support, and summer recreation. Extend the reserve discipline by asking departments to submit Q4 purchase-order closeout plans no later than November 5 so year-end obligations do not surprise the forecast. For Council, frame the 0.2-point decline as normal seasonal movement, while still showing the watch-item list that Finance is actively managing.

periods.analysis: Harborview closed 2025-Q4 at 19.1%, a 0.5 percentage point decrease from 19.6%, and the result remains green above the >=16% threshold. This is the largest decline in the arc so far, but it is still managed and traceable to planned year-end activity, including the storm-readiness equipment buy, final grant-match posting for the Bayfront Trail segment, and higher December mutual-aid backfill costs. Finance completed the reserve calculation after audit workpaper tie-out WP-GF-12, and the value stayed stable through the final departmental review, which is a good data-quality signal. The narrative for Council should be balanced: we used some capacity for approved priorities, but we did not compromise the City’s structural reserve posture.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green position by carrying forward the year-end reserve bridge into the audit presentation, with one-time uses separated from operating base changes. Extend the discipline by requiring any proposed midyear additions in early 2026 to identify an offset, a one-time funding source, or a clear reason to use reserves while staying above policy. Finance should schedule a 30-minute director huddle before the Q1 forecast so departments understand the 19.1% starting point and the Council-facing message is consistent.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q1, reserves improved to 19.3%, up 0.2 percentage points from 19.1%, returning the measure to an upward path while remaining green against the >=16% target. The recovery was modest but useful, supported by early property-tax apportionment, lower-than-budgeted winter storm response costs, and delayed hiring in three non-safety classifications. Finance also moved the reserve dashboard refresh into the standard month-end close checklist, which reduced manual follow-up and gave departments an earlier chance to confirm their numbers. After the planned Q4 draw, this quarter shows Council that Harborview can absorb approved spending and still rebuild reserves through disciplined operations.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the reserve dashboard tied to month-end close, not as a separate after-the-fact exercise. Extend the improvement by converting the delayed-hiring savings into a formal Q2 forecast adjustment rather than letting it sit unassigned in departmental lines. Ask Human Resources and Finance to jointly flag which vacancies are timing savings versus true ongoing savings before the next Council budget workshop.

periods.analysis: Harborview reached 20.1% in 2026-Q2, a 0.8 percentage point increase from 19.3%, and is firmly green above the >=16% target. This is the strongest result in the eight-quarter arc, driven by favorable spring revenues, the closeout of prior-year encumbrances on vendor accounts V-1842 and V-2197, and continued control of departmental operating budgets. The movement from 19.1% at 2025-Q4 to 20.1% now gives Council a clear fiscal stewardship message: reserves were used thoughtfully, then replenished without service disruption. The AA-rated position is reinforced here, but the tone should stay disciplined—we are in a strong place because teams met deadlines, documented assumptions, and avoided turning one-time strength into recurring commitments.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by adopting 20.1% as the planning baseline for the next quarterly forecast and preserving the >=16% policy floor as the non-negotiable minimum. Extend the strength by recommending a Council-approved reserve strategy: maintain operating reserves, assign a limited one-time amount to capital or grant-match needs, and leave recurring program expansions to the normal budget process. Finance should publish a concise eight-quarter reserve trend for the budget retreat so departments see how their closeout discipline contributed to this result.

periods.analysis: Reserves are 18.3%, down from 18.6% but still above the 17% target. A favorable reserve position should not be presented as committed funding for delayed capital work.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the reserve floor and distinguish approved capital allocations from potential grant funding in the briefing book.
